beats.trigger: Getting Going
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: With the right guardrails, you create output that's genuinely yours, not generic.
beats.got: nothing new. This is the usual promise on the first slide.

beats.trigger: Build a snake game as HTML.
beats.got: Homework before the first session. I wonder who did it, and my calendar is full.

beats.trigger: **Package** the guardrails as reusable rules
beats.got: nothing new. It's a verb list, the way every programme opens.

beats.trigger: where did LLM output on your own work come out generic, and what made it feel like yours?
beats.got: A fair question. I have seen generic output and can answer it from my own work.

beats.trigger: The same question. Two answers. What makes the difference?
beats.got: A teaser. Fine, show me.

beats.trigger: The first exchange became context.
beats.got: Rome and the Finnish lake change the dinner suggestion. I could try that tonight, and it's cheap.

beats.trigger: Your first prompt and its answer are part of the input to the second prompt.
beats.got: The model rereads everything each time, so what I put first steers what comes after. Plain mechanics, no hype.

beats.trigger: The suggestion shifts: heart-healthy, low-sodium, vegetable-forward.
beats.got: Telling it who I am changes the answer. Obvious once said, but I can verify it myself.

beats.trigger: Tools, goals, checks, boundaries, and loops come later and depend on it.
beats.got: nothing new. It's a roadmap slide with a list of things I'll hear about later.

beats.trigger: You can put the context in a file the agent reads at the start of every session.
beats.got: Standing instructions live in a file. That's useful if it works, and I'll see.

beats.trigger: Change the context, watch the agent's output shift, then package what you learned for the next session.
beats.got: 45 minutes making a personal website. A strange choice for a telecom director, but I'll do it.

beats.trigger: It works, but it's generic.
beats.got: A page built from my LinkedIn text, competent and bland. It's a fair baseline, and I haven't done anything hard yet.

beats.trigger: A colleague who lands on it should think *"this is the person I want to work with more, on the things they're great at,"*
beats.got: The site is supposed to make colleagues like me. I don't need that from a website.

beats.trigger: The LLM already knows StoryBrand, so you don't reproduce the questions.
beats.got: I can name a framework and it already knows it. That is a handy shortcut, and also the reverse of Jobs-to-be-Done.

beats.trigger: The agent walks you through the five tuned beats.
beats.got: It asks me five questions, I answer, and it rebuilds the page. A framework with a long label, but fine.

beats.trigger: Your strengths shape how the whole site sounds.
beats.got: I give it a few strengths and the tone changes. I didn't need to be told to expect that.

beats.trigger: Most people can list what drives them mad at work in thirty seconds, but stall for five minutes on what they're great at.
beats.got: True of me. I can list what I hate faster than what I'm good at.

beats.trigger: Not categories ("bureaucracy") but actual things ("meetings where nobody disagrees,"
beats.got: My hate list was specific and gave the page edge. I had plenty to give it, and it came out sharper than the strengths version.

beats.trigger: The agent is reading its own work where it wrote it, and LLMs go easy on their own output.
beats.got: The tool says its own self-review is unreliable and tells me how to work around it. Candid, and that earns attention.

beats.trigger: *"Make it look like Stripe's design language"*
beats.got: I can name a site and get its look. Restyling three versions in minutes is something that wasn't possible two years ago.

beats.trigger: The chat summary rounds corners; the file is what travels
beats.got: I get a rules file describing how I did it, and I'm told to push back on what's wrong. Sensible, but the file has to prove itself.

beats.trigger: The more specific the context, the more the output is yours.
beats.got: More specific input gives more specific output. Fine, but it is short of a discovery.

beats.trigger: anywhere the question is "is this genuinely ours or just fine?"
beats.got: It claims the same move works for proposals and compliance reviews. Plausible, but I haven't seen it done on any of those.

beats.trigger: Iterate and Learn
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The move: change something, notice what shifted, adjust, build again.
beats.got: nothing new. It's the old iterate-and-learn loop with a new object.

beats.trigger: Agreeable answers won the round the model was tuned on.
beats.got: The model flatters itself because agreeable answers were rewarded in training. A refreshingly honest limit.

beats.trigger: Read what comes back as a claim about the work, not a verdict on it.
beats.got: Treat an agent's report as a claim to check. I already do that with my own team's status reports.

beats.trigger: Only you could catch a wrong line about you, which is why your own profile is the place to start.
beats.got: The test case worked because I know my own subject. Fair, though it doesn't say how this holds up on my business.

beats.trigger: **Mental models only come from doing.**
beats.got: Nobody knows where this is going, which is the honest part. The rest, a 'little piece of felt experience', is the mindset talk I tune out.

beats.trigger: Expect the generation rules to change a lot. The first pass is rarely right.
beats.got: The agent reviews the rules file against the session. A second pass is how this gets better, and they say so openly.

beats.trigger: **compound interest on a rule file.**
beats.got: Repeat the loop on every file. The slogan is pure programme vocabulary.

beats.trigger: Your gut on what is uniquely you carries more weight than the agent's.
beats.got: A second, fresh reader sees only the site. My judgement still outranks the machine's, and I can test that.

beats.trigger: Your domain expertise is the test.
beats.got: Three bullets that say the same thing as the whole session. Acceptable summary.

beats.trigger: Bring a live challenge and working access to Confluence and OneDrive.
beats.got: More homework. Access to Confluence will take me a week from IT.

beats.trigger: Karpathy's LLM Wiki post; Lindenberg's memory-architecture piece, optional.
beats.got: nothing new. Two more reading items I won't open.

beats.trigger: leave yourself a three-line readiness note.
beats.got: A to-do list for the next session. I carry plenty of those.

beats.trigger: If stuck, scan your next two weeks of calendar; the biggest unresolved item is usually your challenge.
beats.got: Pick a real unsolved problem from my calendar for the memory exercise. That is a practical way to choose, and I have several.

beats.trigger: If a connector needs admin approval, tell the training coordinator and keep going.
beats.got: Connecting this to company systems means IT and data protection get involved, and they will have views.

beats.trigger: Before it writes anything, ask it for a plan and approve or revise it first.
beats.got: Ask for a plan and approve it before the agent changes files. A sensible control I would want anyway.

beats.trigger: If a line is blank, name a fallback; do not fill it with a plausible answer.
beats.got: Write a three-line handoff file. The rule not to bluff with a plausible answer is the one thing in it I liked.

beats.trigger: a useful system is a living pile of text the agent can read, maintain, and improve.
beats.got: nothing new. Another reading assignment, and I won't get to it.

beats.trigger: The output now travels with a file the agent re-reads next time.
beats.got: Next time builds a memory on that. We'll see if module 2 shows more than module 1.

take_homes: What I tell the model first changes what it says next. I saw it with the Rome and Finland dinner example, and I can check it myself.
Naming a framework or a famous site gets me a usable first draft fast. Specific input, like my real hate list, gave a sharper result than the polite strengths list.
The agent's review of its own work is too kind, so I check it against my own knowledge or get a cold second read.

monday.move: Probably nothing formal. If a free half hour appears, I might paste a real strategy memo into a chat with a role and a short hate list and see whether the result is any less generic.
monday.when: maybe later this week, not Monday
monday.stop_condition: The output reads like the generic version again, or it needs more than 20 minutes to get anywhere.
monday.blocker: Calendar full of steering groups, plus the Confluence access request I haven't filed.

misconception.why: Not changed, but dented. The session said what doesn't work (self-review is unreliable) and let me test a claim myself, which none of the last three programmes did. I still think this might blow over, but the context mechanism is real and cheap enough to try.

one_line: Less fluff than the last programmes. I made a website from my LinkedIn, and the one useful thing was a candid note that the machine flatters its own work.
